analysis.one_liner: Replaces across-the-board budget cuts with cuts to food assistance, Medicaid, financial regulation, and federal workers' benefits.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 218-199 on May 10, 2012, with all 218 yes votes from Republicans and none from Democrats; the Senate placed it on its calendar, never voted on it, and it died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill was House Republicans' answer to the automatic across-the-board spending cuts (the 'sequester') scheduled to hit in January 2013. Instead of letting those cuts fall on the Pentagon, it cancelled them and made up the money by cutting the SNAP food program, repealing health care and prevention funding, letting states cut Medicaid and CHIP eligibility, ending the HAMP mortgage-modification program, making federal employees pay more into their own retirements, capping medical malpractice awards, and repealing parts of the Dodd-Frank financial law that handle failing big banks and fund the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and large financial firms, which would have lost the Dodd-Frank orderly-liquidation authority and the Office of Financial Research and seen the CFPB subject to annual appropriations; doctors and malpractice insurers, who would gain the $250,000 damage caps; the defense budget, which was exempted from the sequester; and deficit-focused taxpayers generally.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks, malpractice defendants, and the defense budget

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Dodd-Frank's orderly-liquidation authority and its Orderly Liquidation Fund — the process for winding down a failing large financial company outside bankruptcy — and eliminates the Office of Financial Research.

Ends the Federal Reserve's automatic funding transfer to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and repeals its Victims Relief Fund, subjecting the bureau to the annual appropriations process instead.
Caps noneconomic damages in health care lawsuits at $250,000, limits punitive damages, and restricts lawyers' contingent fees.
Nullifies the fiscal 2013 sequestration order for defense spending and removes veterans' medical care from the accounts subject to sequester.

Terminates HAMP, which the bill's own findings note had produced 782,609 permanent mortgage modifications against a goal of 3 to 4 million, freeing an estimated $2.84 billion for deficit reduction, while providing no replacement foreclosure help beyond a Sense of Congress that banks 'encourage' loan modifications.

analysis.who_pays: Low-income households, who lose SNAP categorical eligibility, the standard utility allowance, Puerto Rico and American Samoa benefit increases, and the Title XX social services block grants; Medicaid and CHIP beneficiaries, whose federal eligibility protections are repealed so states can cut enrollment; homeowners facing foreclosure, who lose HAMP; federal workers, who pay 5% of salary more into retirement over five years and lose the annuity supplement if newly hired; and flood insurance policyholders, whose annual premium increases can now run to 20% with faster phase-outs of subsidized rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food-stamp recipients, Medicaid patients, federal workers

drawbacks.text: Cuts fall on nutrition and health programs: SNAP categorical eligibility is limited to households receiving cash assistance, the standard utility allowance is restricted, and Title XX social services block grants are repealed outright.

Repeals the Affordable Care Act's Prevention and Public Health Fund, exchange-planning grants, and CO-OP program funding, and repeals Medicaid and CHIP maintenance-of-effort rules that barred states from cutting eligibility.
Federal employees' take-home pay drops by up to 5% of salary over five years through higher retirement contributions, and the FERS annuity supplement is eliminated for anyone hired after 2012.
Flood insurance premiums can rise up to 20% per year under the bill (up from 10%), and full actuarial rates phase in for second homes, homes sold to new owners, and repeatedly flooded properties.

House Democrats' motion to recommit — which would have barred former Members of Congress who are registered lobbyists with salaries over $1 million from federal retirement benefits — was defeated 170-232.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does reduce deficits without new revenue, and HAMP had a documented record of underperformance, so some cuts (state bonus programs, unspent HAMP funds) target genuine slack. But the largest savings come from nutrition assistance, health coverage protections, prevention funding, financial-regulation enforcement, and federal workers' compensation, while the defense budget is shielded — so the burden lands heavily on households with the least, and the bill was written to a closed rule with no amendments allowed.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a straight party-line vote, but the Senate simply put it on its calendar and never brought it up, and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Budget Committee, chaired by Paul Ryan, reported the bill as an original measure on May 9, 2012, the day after it was introduced.
The Rules Committee's rule (H. Res. 648) allowed only two hours of debate, closed the bill to amendments, and waived all points of order against its provisions.
On final passage the vote was 218-199: all 218 yes votes came from Republicans, with 16 Republicans and 183 voting Democrats opposed, and no Democrat voting yes.

Before passage, Democrats' motion to recommit with instructions to add a bar on former Members who are registered lobbyists earning over $1 million from federal retirement benefits failed 170-232, with 168 of 190 voting Democrats for it and 228 of 241 voting Republicans against.
The Senate received the bill on May 14, 2012, read it twice, and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders; no further action was ever taken.
The bill carried a reconciliation instruction from the fiscal 2013 budget resolution, which is what allowed its single fiscal title to combine so many unrelated cuts into one package.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-income households kept their SNAP benefits and social services block grants, federal workers kept their retirement contributions unchanged, and Wall Street kept the Dodd-Frank liquidation authority and the CFPB's independent funding. The trade-off was that the January 2013 defense sequester was left unresolved by this route.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food-assistance recipients; Wall Street kept Dodd-Frank

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split 218-199 entirely by party — Republicans 218-16 in favor, Democrats 0-183 — and the motion to recommit split similarly (Democrats 168-4 for it, Republicans 228-2 against).

industries.note: The bill repeals Dodd-Frank's orderly-liquidation authority for failing large financial companies, the Office of Financial Research, and the CFPB's independent Fed funding. Removing the liquidation process shifts failing-firm resolution back toward bankruptcy, where creditors have more leverage, and the funding change gives future Congresses a lever to starve the consumer regulator.

industries.industry: Medical malpractice insurers and health care providers
industries.note: Caps noneconomic damages at $250,000, limits punitive damages, and restricts attorney fees in health care lawsuits. Injured patients with large non-economic losses would recover less; malpractice insurers and providers pay less.

Repeals funding for the CO-OP program, which was designed to create nonprofit insurers to compete in individual and small-group markets, and rescinds unobligated exchange-planning grants, reducing competition and the ACA's buildout.

The bill requires lenders to accept qualifying private flood insurance and directs studies of privatizing the National Flood Insurance Program. Homeowners gain force-placed-insurance refunds but face a higher annual premium-increase cap of 20% and faster phase-outs of subsidized rates.
The bill nullifies the fiscal 2013 defense sequestration and combines security and nonsecurity spending limits, shifting the burden of deficit reduction away from the Pentagon budget.

Federal workers and Members of Congress would pay up to 5% of salary more into retirement over five years, and new hires would lose the FERS annuity supplement — effectively a pay cut for roughly two million workers and their families.
HAMP's termination ends federal pressure on servicers to modify loans, removing a program that required lender participation, while leaving foreclosure prevention to voluntary bank action.
